speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
This is something upon which we have changed our minds. What is more, of course, as the hon. member for Essex East reminds me, the Canadian Citizenship Act was a monument to the Mackenzie King government and to the hon. member for Essex East. An improvement in the act was made by the hon. lady when she introduced her bill, and we said so at the time. We could not understand why she did not go the whole way, and when we get back into office we intend to go the whole way unless that has been done in the meantime by this government which professes to have such a regard for our rights, our liberties and our citizenship. If they will do it I will applaud

them. The Prime Minister need have no doubt how I will vote on the measure; I shall vote for it.
I should like to go back very briefly, because I believe I have very few minutes left, to the arguments of the Minister of Justice and the arguments of my hon. friend from Laurier. Our position, it seems to me, is very simple and very clear. We believe the best course the government could take would have been to consult the provincial governments to see if it might not have been possible to agree upon an amendment to the constitution which would have safeguarded human rights and fundamental freedoms against all jurisdictions by agreement; not by centralization, not by force, not by a kind of usurpation of jurisdiction at which the Prime Minister seemed to be hinting in 1947. I readily admit it might not have been possible to succeed. I think the prospects have been vastly improved in the last couple of weeks. We have one or two Liberal governments with which it would be easier to deal than some of the governments they replaced, but it might still be a very difficult thing to do.
However, we might be able to do both things at once. We might be able, at the same time, to agree on a national bill of rights for all Canadians in all jurisdictions and on a method to amend our constitution here at home. We might be able to put it all in a package, and that would be the ideal. I think this ought to be the ideal of everybody in the house. Perhaps we could not realize it, but if we could get agreement on the bill of rights what would be wrong with going to Westminster and having it put into the British North America Act?
This is what my right hon. friend Mr. St. Laurent did in 1949, when he put the use of the French language beyond peradventure by a constitutional amendment and made the other amendments to which my hon. friend from Laurier referred. This is what happened at that time. If you can go to Westminster to change the status of county court judges, which status has been regarded as the prerogative of this parliament since 1867, why would it be such a terrible thing to go to Westminster to maintain the freedoms and fundamental rights of all Canadians? The argument of the Minister of Justice is really so tawdry that it is hardly worthy of reply.
If that were not possible, if indeed this second best method of the Prime Minister's is all we can hope for, surely at least advantage could have been taken of the amendment to the British North America Act of 1949, and we could have had this bill as an act to amend the British North America
Human Rights
Act with the bill of rights as the subtitle. I admit that under the law there would have been no difference whatever; it would have been precisely the same thing. However, the mere fact of calling it an amendment to the British North America Act, the mere act of recognizing it for what it ought to be, a part of our fundamental constitution, would, as my hon. friend from Essex East said in an intervention this morning, have given it dignity, would have given it added respect. This is not a very great point, but it is a point.
If the government insist upon continuing in the way they are going on, then I do not see that it will do any harm and it may do a very small amount of good to have once more reiterated these historic British freedoms which have never been questioned in peacetime since 1867 so far as this parliament is concerned, whatever may unfortunately have happened on a few occasions in some legislatures.
In conclusion may I say that I have sought to give to this subject the importance it deserves, and I urge the Prime Minister very strongly to give the utmost consideration to those suggestions which were put forward by my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition, which would give to this bill more content than it now has.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel rather humble in rising to speak in the debate on Bill No. C-79, an act for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, particularly after listening on Monday and Tuesday of this week to the heights and then again the depths of oratory. Despite the many arguments which have been advanced by hon. members of the opposition-that such a bill does not go far enough in its protection of these rights; that this bill is not required; that the present act, as the hon. member who just preceded me said, is thin gruel-it is my firm belief that as long as the present government is in office and is headed by the right hon. gentleman who is our Prime Minister, the rights of the individual will be fully protected, as stated in clause 2 of the bill. '
I had intended, Mr. Speaker, to make reference to what happened during and after the war to Canadians of Japanese origin, but a considerable amount has been said on that subject and it will not be necessary for me to say more except that in my lifetime Canadians have fought and died in two world wars for the protection of the rights and the freedoms of the individual. I am proud to say that I myself served for 12 years in His Majesty's and Her Majesty's forces for the protection of those rights. I would feel that

Human Rights
such service had been in vain for my children and their children were it not for this protection we are now going to get as a result of this bill.
I should like to say that one of my comrades in the last war was the son of a Japanese Canadian, who was born in Canada, whose father had come to Canada and worked for the privilege of Canadian citizenship. I can well recall the shock, amazement and hurt of that comrade of mine when his people were deprived of everything they had given their lifetime to acquire, and were shoved away without even the bare necessities of life.
To many people in many lands Canada stands out as a beacon of hope in their search for a home where freedom is the rule and is protected. A further assurance of this freedom will be given by this bill. In the second latest issue of the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget there appeared a short poem which I should like to read into the record. It makes a plea for that brotherhood which is enjoyed in Canada by Canadians of many origins. The poem reads as follows: Plea for Brotherhood The same skies arch above us.
The peoples of all the earth;
The same dear Father loves us,
Though varied our station and birth;
Oh, teach us, dear Heavenly Father,
That together we stand or fall,
That we but live in separate rooms-
The same roof covers all.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I myself am a first generation Canadian. My father was born in Dundee, Scotland and my mother in London, England. They came to Canada as young people. I consider myself to be wholly Canadian. I should like to repeat the pledge made by the Prime Minister as it appears at page 5649 of Hansard of July 1:
X am a Canadian, a free Canadian, free to speak without fear, free to worship God in my own way, free to stand for what I think right, free to oppose what I believe wrong, free to choose those who shall govern my country. This heritage of freedom I pledge to uphold for myself and all mankind.
I express the hope that such a pledge will be taken by all Canadians now and in the future.

speechtext:
When one on in years sits in his seat and listens to the debate it naturally prompts recollections of one's reading of history and recollections and memories of one's personal experiences. When I was listening to the Prime Minister's remarks in moving second reading of this bill I could not help but think of the history of Magna Carta in 1215, the bill of rights in 1689, the British North America Act in 1867, the Statute of Westminster in 1931, the declaration of the prime ministers of the commonwealth in 1944 and the declaration of human rights and fundamental freedoms made by the United Nations just a few years ago.
When we discuss this subject-that is those who are particularly interested in it-I think we must admit that while there has always been a core of people concerned with the preservation and extension of human rights and fundamental freedoms, unfortunately there are too many people who accept those rights and freedoms without any sense of responsibility for maintaining them or their improvement. However, I am sure we all

realize that Canadian civilization draws its ideas on this extremely important question primarily from Great Britain and France and also to a lesser extent from a number of other countries.
When the Prime Minister was speaking, thinking in terms of history I could not help recalling my reading of the experiences of the Topuddle martyrs, of Keir Hardie's life, of the contributions that Mr. Campbell Ban-nerman and Mr. Lloyd George, former prime ministers of Great Britain, made to this question in the House of Commons in London and in British public life, and also some well-known, important Tories. I would not for one moment suggest that throughout the years members of one party had been the only persons to defend human rights and fundamental freedoms.
I would not for a moment suggest that members of one party have been the only persons to defend human rights and fundamental freedoms, because I am sure many of us have read of the activities of the Duchess of Atholl, a well-known Tory in some respects, who took a great interest in this question. Then there was the Countess of Warwick, a Tory in many respects in her early days until she was influenced by some evangelical preacher and socialist contacts. She was another aristocrat who became interested in the preservation of fundamental rights and human freedoms.
I think that at this point it would be appropriate to mention that there seems to be some instinct among the British peoples in all parties which causes them to recognize the value of democracy and to understand the meaning of freedom and its foundations. I think it would be appropriate at this time in view of the unfortunate death of the Right Hon. Aneurin Bevan to mention that I heard him speak in the House of Commons in November, 1946, when he paid a magnificent tribute to the Right Hon. Winston Churchill. Mr. Churchill was then on the first seat to the right of the front government benches. I was in the gallery, listening with interest, and I heard Mr. Bevan pay tribute to the former prime minister of Great Britain. During most of the time Mr. Bevan was speaking the former prime minister was applauding most heartily. I think this indicates the essence of what democracy stands for, when two men, at opposite ends of the poll as far as economics and, possibly, as far as social origins are concerned, are willing to pay tribute to each other's ability and to the contribution they have made to the country and to the welfare of the state.
At the same time I had the happy experience of being entertained at the Hurling-ham club. I am not used to going to such 79951-0-373
Human Rights
places, because I am a humble person, but I was invited one Sunday by members of the House of Lords who kindly put on a special dinner for me at the club. I had an interesting time explaining the Canadian situation to them and explaining what the C.C.F. stood for and its position in relation to the Labour party. I remember one ancient peer-he was a member of the peerage, not the beerage-saying this, this incident comes to mind because it is connected with Mr. Aneurin Bevan: He said: "you know, that man has said some very annoying things on occasions, at times some nasty things but really he is a very decent fellow. He is very honest, he has strong socialist convictions but he is a sound democrat. You know, he is an excellent chap to go on a party with once in a while." That, I think, could only happen in a country like Great Britain where the principles we have talked about here in the last two or three days are respected, and practised.
To return to Canadian history, I think no one who has spoken so far in this debate has mentioned names of persons in recent Canadian history who have been staunch defenders of human rights and fundamental freedoms. I am sure everyone would wish mention to be made of the late Mr. J. S. Woodsworth's magnificent contribution and in particular his fight in opposition to section 98 of the Criminal Code during and after the Winnipeg strike-a man who went to jail because he believed in human rights. Then there was William Irvine who served in this house for a good many years. He is still active, and I understand that at the present time he is travelling abroad in order to extend his knowledge of international conditions and world affairs. I could also mention the father of the present hon. member for Vancouver East, Mr. Ernest Winch, who spent all his life in support of the principles we are discussing this afternoon.
We all know, in more recent years particularly, of the stand taken by Mr. M. J. Cold-well and his defence of the principles about which we are now speaking, and I wish, also, to give credit to the Senate, because I like to give credit where it is due. I was delighted last year when the Senate took a strong stand in opposition to representatives of the private power companies of British Columbia who came to the Senate committee and urged it to recommend an amendment to an act which had been passed by this parliament. The act provided in one of its sections that taxation of the export of power should be by law instead of by order in council. These private power companies came to the Senate committee and urged that this should be changed so that

Human Rights
taxation on the export of power would be by order in council so that they would have an opportunity to come before any government and negotiate the taxes they would pay. I was very pleased on reading the minutes of the Senate to notice that the members of both parties in that chamber unitedly opposed the suggestion made by the private power companies of British Columbia in this respect.
As far as I personally am concerned I have always been interested in these questions. As a boy I remember when the miners in the Kootenays were on strike there was a telephone line between Silverton and San-don, two small mining towns in that area, and in order that the mine owners should not know what the conversation was between the union locals concerned the workers got two Gaelic speaking miners from Cape Breton to carry on the necessary conversations. It was reported to the late Mr. Bowser, then attorney general, that there were subversive foreign elements in control of the strike, and Mr. Bowser was going to send the militia to stop it. Anyway the uncle of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, (Mr. Green), who was then commissioner of works in British Columbia went straight to Victoria and spoke up for those miners. He made it clear that there were no subversive or foreign elements connected with this strike, but that these were men only exercising democratic rights. Thus he persuaded the government not to send in the troops. I mention this because the gentleman in question was a well-known Conservative.
In my own experience I know of two prominent Liberals who insisted on the right of a socialist to speak in a small community Where the local board of trade had arranged to have him thrown into the lake when he arrived at the dock on the steamer.
There are many others in all parties, though possibly they are in a minority, who have an instinct for doing this sort of thing and defending the principles we are now discussing. All these people, whether socialists or Liberals or Conservatives, were moved by an elemental force, a spirit proceeding from a knowledge of principles, honesty and from conviction. People of that type did not rely on a multigraph machine or on advertising agencies to spread their views and ideas in the community and influence others. The Prime Minister CMr. Diefenbaker)-and I give him full credit-has shown a public interest in the question since about 1942, I understand, by his speeches in this house, by resolutions introduced into this house, and by speeches outside the house.

When the Prime Minister introduced the second reading of the bill the stage was well set. It was confederation day. There was the glamour and glitter of the ceremony of the previous evening and the anticipation of the coming afternoon. There were crowded galleries showing the interest of the public in this question. We all listened to his words with great attention.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister sipped from the goblet of parliamentary sublimity sip by sip with relish, the only fly in the ointment being that fearless trumpet-voiced stinging nettle from the riding of Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).
This debate deals with a principle with which an increasing number of Canadians are concerned. The Prime Minister agreed with an earlier opposition spokesman who said that the opposition has the responsibility of criticism. I will now summarize our criticism of this bill, not for the sake of repetition but to have it appear on the record in relation to our intentions.
The first criticism is the lateness of the session for the introduction of the bill. The committee will not have sufficient time to deal with it properly. We want the committee to take ample time to examine it so all interested organizations can present their views.
The second criticism is that the government did not consult the provinces. It is not enough to say the experience of the past justifies inaction in that respect.
The third criticism is that the bill is weak from a legal point of view.
The fourth criticism is that it does not guarantee the rights mentioned. It is a declaration without guarantees.
The fifth criticism is that there is no protection provided for economic freedom.
We are laymen in this group with no legal training. Therefore in discussing bills of this kind we have to rely on information from experts in the field. In that connection I will quote from a book entitled "Civil Liberties and Canadian Federalism" by F. R. Scott, a prominent member of the C.C.F. and a noted authority on constitutional law. Although the book was published in 1959 it deals with the principle of the Prime Minister's bill introduced last year, and this one is similar. I will quote one paragraph:
I conclude therefore that this bill has perhaps educational value; it will stand as a solemn affirmation of democratic beliefs; it spells out a number of specific rights in a detailed way. It is a bill of rights for all Canadians, yes, because all Canadians come under some federal law. But it is a very partial bill, applicable only in peacetime, no stronger

than the self-restraint of our federal members of parliament at any given moment, and inapplicable to provincial legislatures. Moreover it is confined to political and personal freedoms; it makes no attempt to protect other human rights, like the right to non-discrimination in employment. Cultural and economic rights are also omitted.
The Prime Minister mentioned past experience as justification for not consulting the provinces. We believe he should have included these principles in the constitution covering only those fields over which parliament has jurisdiction while at the same time urging the provinces to pass enabling legislation, as it were bills of rights in the various provinces, so that in time all Canadians would be covered by the umbrella of federal and provincial legislation. There has been criticism all across the country by individuals, organizations and editors along the lines voiced by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue).
We want the provinces to be with us in working toward the development of legislation enshrining these great historic principles in our constitution and provincial statutes. We intend to support the bill as the first instalment of a program that soon will guarantee to all Canadians their fundamental rights and human freedoms. We hope the bill goes to committee and that the committee will find some inspiration from the debate on second reading. We recommend the amendments we have advancd which will strengthen the language of the bill.
In Great Britain these rights and freedoms have been accepted for centuries based on historic legal documents, tradition, precedence, practice and the spirit of the people. Some ask why, in view of the experience in countries like Great Britain, do we need a bill of rights. I realize no bill of rights is effective without the understanding and support of the people it is intended to serve. However in our industrial society conditions are rapidly changing. You cannot change the total area or volume of the earth. They are constant. You cannot change the total power in the world or in any country. They are constant.
In our industrial society the sources of these powers are changing quickly as a result of the industrial revolution. First, governments require and obtain more and more power to do the things necessary for the people and country. Second, some segments of our economy are obtaining more and more power every year and try to use it. An example was a group of representatives of private power companies of British Columbia who attempted to persuade the Senate to vote for taxation by order in council. These monopolists are becoming stronger and bolder every year. We in this group believe that 79951-0-373J
Human Rights
in addition to the example provided by the experience in Great Britain and other countries the time has come to enshrine in our constitution the human rights and fundamental freedoms we aim to preserve and extend. The preservation of freedom in any society or in any country, regardless of bills of rights, sections in the constitutions, in the last analysis depends on the spirit of the people and their eternal vigilance and understanding.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say we will look forward to the report of the committee that will study this most important bill and at that time we will take advantage of the opportunity to express our opinions on the committee's report.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to clear up a matter which was raised this morning by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who accused my department of doing something incorrectly by order in council. The hon. member suggested that I had been responsible for an improper action in that an order in council under the Aeronautics Act had been passed to circumvent the air transport board. This is a complete misunderstanding both of the facts and of the law. The suggestion that this order in council was passed in order to make it unnecessary for a finding of public convenience and necessity to be made is incorrect.
The removal of the requirement for a finding of public convenience and necessity by the air transport board with regard to all classes of service, other than scheduled services, was, in fact, made under the Aeronautic Act by the previous administration in 1954, on the recommendation of the transport board. I would refer the hon. member to the commercial air service's regulations, P.C. 1954 2032, in section 6, subsection 1, which substituted a finding of public interest for all services other than class 1 scheduled services. The further amendment in January by P.C. 1960 65, was made, in fact, on the recommendation of the air transport board, and restated this position, namely the need for a finding of public interest in lieu of public necessity, but removed from this aircraft charter services in groups B and C, medium to light aircraft, so that the board on its own recommendation was not required in these classes of service to make a finding of either public necessity or public interest; that is, no particular finding need be made in regard to these categories of licence, class 4, groups B and C. This change, on the recommendation of the air transport board, was made quite properly under section 13 of the Aeronautics Act.

Human Rights
This was done at the time I announced as a matter of government policy, as a more liberal approach to the granting of group B licences as had previously been done in the case of group C.
As for the suggestion that the minister has assumed a role of interfering with the air transport board, I refute this completely. I have the fullest faith in this board. It is my intent and practice to allow the air transport board to proceed without interference on my part to carry out its judicial functions under the Aeronautics Act in giving effect to the aviation policy of the government.
Subsection (1) of section 15 of the Aeronautics Act provides, however, that the board must have the approval of the minister for the issuance of a licence to operate a commercial air service; while subsections (9) and (11) of the same section provide that any air carrier has a right of appeal to the minister against the decisions of the board. These overriding powers granted the minister were inserted in the Aeronautics Act by the previous administration, presumably for a specific purpose; in fact, I assume the reason is similar to the reason behind the statutory provisions which allow a right of appeal to the governor in council in regard to certain types of decisions made by the board of transport commissioners.
It is my view that the minister should leave the air transport board a free hand in carrying out its judicial and regulatory duties, but that parliament, at the request of the previous administration, inserted these provisions in the Aeronautics Act which give the minister and the government power, if it should be his view and that of the government that the national interest requires the minister to exercise his special powers in regard to licensing policy in accordance with normal judicial procedure and with the law.

Mr. Speaker, many members have dealt quite fully with the wording and intent of Bill No. C-79. I will not attempt to repeat those statements which are now on record for future generations to read. I make special reference to the very full and clear outline of the bill by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) today.
Like other speakers, I am proud to be a member of this parliament, to be in this third session of the 24th parliament to assist in the passing of this bill for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
I feel I must take this opportunity to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on his sponsorship of this long-awaited measure, the importance of which even opposition speakers have acknowledged and emphasized by their actions, if not by their words. Reference to and outline of the measure at an earlier session, and probable passage at this session after more than a year of consideration by Canadians, individually and in groups, and by organizations, will be one of the highlights of the Prime Minister's parliamentary career.
The stand of the official opposition in this debate has been one of criticism apparently merely for the sake of criticism. This was shown by the vote on the C.C.F. amendment which would have killed the bill for this session. After all their protestations and faultfinding the Liberals voted to keep the bill before the house rather than have it blocked by the C.C.F. In this it would appear they knew they were meeting the wishes of the people. Most of the criticism of opposition speakers has been along the one line. They say the wording of the bill is unimaginative and uninspiring. Here again they offer carping criticism apparently, as I said before, merely for the sake of criticism. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice have answered those minor criticisms very effectively.
The Prime Minister has said that the wording of this bill is deliberately short and specific to make the intent completely clear and easily understood by all. In a dozen or more lines are outlined and guaranteed our basic freedoms in so far as the powers of the federal parliament are concerned. As the explanatory notes state, part I provides for the establishment of a bill of rights for Canada and part II provides for the continuation in modified form of authority to deal effectively with war, invasion or insurrection.
I do not find the brief wording of the bill unimaginative and uninspiring. I can see

school children learning at an early age this statement of human rights and fundamental freedoms in our free democracy. They will repeat for their teachers that under the Canadian bill of rights it is declared that in Canada there shall continue to exist the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, the right of the individual to the protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, together with freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and association and freedom of the press. Such a guarantee of freedom contained in so few words is far from being uninspiring. Even at public school age students by repeating the words I have just cited will realize the meaning of being a free Canadian.
I see no need to alter part I for any window dressing of words as suggested by some opposition speakers. Of course, there is always the possibility of a preamble in more poetic or high-sounding words. It could be something along this line: When, after nearly five score years of confederation, Canadians called for legislative protection against government encroachment on their civil rights a champion of their rights appeared. A reference to the appearance of such a champion would catch the imagination of all and would give a present day setting to events that will certainly be listed in the pages of history. This is merely a suggestion 1 offer for the consideration of the committee that will be considering the bill before third reading.
The privileges of individual rights, Mr. Speaker, involve personal responsibilities and obligations. If I may, I should like to refer to one particular freedom with which I have had some experience, freedom of the press. I must admit that my newspaper experience was in earlier days. In terms of time it might be referred to as B.C., before columnists and before commentators. In those days reporters reported events as they actually happened; factual reporting, we called it. These factual reports of actual events appeared in the news columns. Opinions and personal views appeared on the editorial page and were easily recognized as merely personal views. Scrupulous care was taken to make sure that personal or biased views did not colour the factual reporting.
In its present connotation the word "press", of course, includes radio and television. As found on page 4639 of Hansard for September 5, 1958, the Prime Minister stated when introducing a similar bill:
I would point out that radio as such or broadcasting in general is not included, because freedom of the press has been defined as including freedom respecting broadcasting.
Human Rights
I have two newspaper clippings here from recent editions of my home town paper, the Moose Jaw Times-Herald. One editorial is headed, "Freedom of the Press" and the second, "What a Free Press Means". I believe that excerpts from these articles are well worth putting on the record. From the editorial headed, "Freedom of the Press" I read the following:
-under modem conditions the press is the principal agency by which the ordinary man receives the information he needs to judge the actions of his rulers and make up his mind on public affairs.
The editorial headed, "What a Free Press Means", reads in part as follows:
In a complex society, few people have the time or opportunity to attend meetings of the various legislative, judicial and administrative bodies which co-ordinate that society. The average man must perforce delegate that task to the journalist.
And further:
The newspaper's job is to winnow the flow of gossip, censure, praise, complaint and proposal, separating the precious grains of fact from the heap of fabrication and fancy.
I should like to repeat those last words, "separating the precious grains of fact from the heap of fabrication and fancy". The first editorial to which I have referred also contains these words:
All liberty ... involves obligations. That of a free newspaper is to be ... thorough, accurate and unbiased in its reporting, sincere and thoughtful in its editorials-
Only such a newspaper, and when I say "newspaper" I also include radio and television, is worthy of the privileges involved in freedom of the press. I believe this sums up the situation very clearly. I am pleased to see some members of the press gallery present. I know their interest in this bill is very great. Again, I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister upon the culmination of his long efforts to bring in a Canadian bill of rights. I am very happy to be here to support his bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take part for a few minutes in the discussion of the recognition and protection of human rights and basic freedoms.
I listened with great attention when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) introduced his bill. The Prime Minister-I will admit-has for many years spoken in this house of legislation which would officially and publicly establish human rights, and has frequently advocated a bill to recognize and preserve those rights.

Human Rights
When the Prime Minister introduced his bill I listened with deep attention. He expressed exalted feelings and also some that were not so high-minded. He spoke feelingly of human freedoms. He said that, in the past, a former government had taken action which was a flagrant denial of those freedoms. He professed to remain above petty politics; however, with a sarcastic smile, he mentioned cases which, according to him, were a violation of human rights and freedoms.
Mr. Speaker, in spite of my limited experience in politics, I have often heard statesmen who excelled in expressing high-minded views. I have also heard some who, at the same time, harboured feelings that were quite the opposite of high-minded. The Prime Minister of this country excels at both.
A bill of rights is something everybody accepts. The Liberal party has been accused of failing to recognize the fact, at the time it held power. The Liberal party has stood judgment in the last two elections. The party chose a new leader who clearly expressed his views on the bill concerning human rights and basic freedoms. Why should we always be reminded of what happened seven, ten and even 12 years ago? The people of Canada have spoken with regard to the administration which ruled this country in 1957. We now have another one, and Liberal members, like their leader, have clearly expressed their views on this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I have been rather surprised by the remarks the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) made this morning. I have great esteem for him, and I say so openly. But, after listening to him, I revised my views with regard to the theory of metempsychosis, or the theory of reincarnation.
Before last June 22, whenever we ventured to criticize the provincial administration, we were often accused of belittling our own province. The Minister of Justice told us this morning that by criticizing the bill of rights, we came close to belittling the people who had elected us, because we were criticizing a legislation which aimed at protecting those freedoms.
There was a man who used to reason in that fashion, and who was premier of my province. I did not bear him any grudge for reasoning that way, but I am amazed that a man of the stamp of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) should be doing so.

The Minister of Justice also accused the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition of playing politics with this bill providing for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. Well then, Mr. Speaker, let us consider again what was said by the one who introduced the bill and who set the tone of this debate. As I said earlier, the Prime Minister of my country expressed lofty feelings in introducing the bill of rights but, on the other hand, he expressed other views that were directly opposite to those lofty feelings and that magnanimity. No one therefore, should be surprised if we recall certain facts in reply to the statement made by the Prime Minister in introducing the bill.
I feel it is the responsibility of the first citizen of this country to inform the people. The Prime Minister of this country should keep above party divisions. In other words, every time he speaks, a statesman who is perfectly conscious of his responsibilities, of his serious responsibilities as the country's first citizen, should teach something to the people. That is his first responsibility. He must be concerned with the general welfare of the people, he must be a leader, and even at the detriment of his political future, must speak his mind. In short, he should speak the truth.
Moreover, I think that, in introducing a bill for the protection of human liberties and fundamental freedoms, the first citizens of this country should rise high above those who sit in the second last or last row in the house- that is my own section. In other words, I could easily forgive myself, or as easily forgive all my colleagues of this section, for playing politics on a question as noble and sublime as this. But I find it very hard to forgive it to the first citizen of my country, the man who holds the highest office in Canada, the man who should set the tone of our debates in this house.
I am glad that the Prime Minister did introduce this bill, however tardily. My colleagues, beginning with my leader, have made quite appropriate and judicious remarks. This does not mean, Mr. Speaker, that when we criticize a bill, we do not approve of its principle. Besides, if there is a man here who should understand this attitude, it is the Prime Minister of Canada, who used to sit on this side of the house. Mr. Robert Muir (Cape Breton North and
Victoria): Mr. Speaker, in opening the remarks I have to make upon this subject may I observe that I believe there are few occasions in the normal routine of parliamentary business which justify a non-partisan approach. However, I believe the measure now before the house provides ample evidence in support of the assertion that on this occasion we are justified in leaving our partisan or sectarian prejudices aside in the consideration of so vital a matter as the preservation and enlargement of fundamental human rights.
Indeed it is on occasions such as the present bill introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) affords that parliament should be seen at its finest, when the gangway that divides this house should shrink under the friendly atmosphere of a common concern and a shared sense of appreciation of the important essentials that in fact unite us. When we come together to consider ways and means of securing even more surely the foundations of human liberty it should be in an atmosphere devoid of 79951-0-374
Human Rights
personal bias or narrow, partisan sectarianism. This is not the time nor the place where the sacred rights of the individual are to be trifled with like pawns on some national chessboard for mere selfish, partisan advantage. In our attempt to guarantee the basic rights of all Canadians let us beware lest we appear to be the pleaders of some special cause or interest. Freedom is indivisible; it must know no boundaries, no limits, no ethnic, racial or religious preferences, apart from the reasonable and equitable demands of reason and responsibility.
Perhaps no subject prompts such widespread interest as the consideration of human rights. Around the world there are precious few bonds that unite nation with nation, but of all the ties that do bind the hearts of mankind none is so strong or so universally appealing as the deep-seated hunger after liberty. It may find expression in different tongues, with different symbols and contrasting motives, but whatever the language the overtones, the melody of liberty is familiar.
I am reminded that in my own riding, as I am sure in other ridings across our land, the heritage of our past recalls for us the truth of this yearning that goes beyond the boundaries of race or creed, or even time itself. Some of the early settlers of Cape Breton came to this land from across the seas in order to escape the tyranny and persecution which afflicted them. They came because the air was free. They came that their children might be born and educated free from the depressing shadows of the countless types of slavery that threatened to envelop and enslave them. They came in quest of personal liberty.
So, I feel that the people I represent are vitally involved in this bill of rights, and I would be remiss in the discharge of my duty to my constituents and to Canada if in a matter that concerns every Canadian I were to remain silent and by that gesture of neglect fail to raise my voice for the cause of freedom.
The bill before this house is a most interesting and significant legislative development. I must at the outset disclaim any pretence of being versed in the legal or constitutional complexities of such a measure, but I respectfully submit that the voice of freedom's followers cannot be confined to the carefully measured syllables of the legal expert alone. On the contrary, our voices must transmit the longings and aspirations, the hopes and fears of all who hunger and thirst after liberty. Perhaps I can add my voice to those of others, and speak, if I may, for the so-called ordinary man in the street, or

Human Rights
woman in the street to whom the legal niceties and constitutional technicalities are a strange and alien tongue.
The bill introduced by the Prime Minister at a previous session and now laid before the house for our consideration deserves the serious attention of every hon. member. I believe it is worth noting that in the very manner in which this measure has been submitted every effort has been made to see that this bill receives the careful, thorough study that its subject matter demands. The Prime Minister when he first introduced this bill in September of 1958 deliberately chose not to press parliament for a decision on this matter. Rather he invited all hon. members, and indeed the nation at large, to use the intervening months for careful study followed by practical, realistic and constructive suggestions as to how the bill could be improved within the framework of our present constitutional abilities.
What have we witnessed since that historic September day? With few exceptions it has been a case of much sound and fury signifying nothing. In almost every case the critical comments have been characterized by a negative, impractical and unrealistic approach. In essence, the critics of this bill have said: It is so far short of the ideal that we cannot stand the thought of having to accept a measure that is less than perfect.
My partisan preferences and genuine admiration for the Prime Minister and leader of my party have not blinded me to the awareness of truth and reality. Indeed, I freely concede that this measure is not perfect. Ideally I could wish that the fundamental legislative guarantees of basic human rights could be both comprehensive and protected from the risk of passing emotion and temporary public displeasure.
We could all wish that Canada's growth and development had reached the stage where we could say that all our constitutional and procedural problems had been solved. We would all agree that such basic assurances as provided in this bill should apply to all Canadians in every part of Canada under whatever jurisdiction. We all desire that such safeguards be so enshrined that the effort required to destroy or amend them would be sufficient to deter all but the genuine need for legitimate reform.
But Canadians must not let these so-called saints of perfection pull the wool over our eyes. Are we for that reason to deny to all Canadians some measure of protection simply because we are not able to achieve the perfect solution? If this view is sound then I submit that confederation was a dismal mistake, the linking of this country by rail

was a foul plot and indeed we could say that every forward step we have taken along the great road of confederation has been a sorry bedraggled series of disasters because we have had to settle for something less than perfection itself.
I cannot subscribe to that view, no matter from what quarter of the house it is proposed. In fact, I rather seriously doubt whether my hon. friends opposite in their own hearts even subscribe to such an obviously discredited philosophy. However, how they vote on this bill will in the final analysis reveal their real beliefs. Canada's history has many examples of honourable compromise and accommodation. In fact it has often been said, rather facetiously I fear, that this is the typically Canadian way to solve a problem.
Before voting on a bill as important, far-reaching and significant as this one we should give careful consideration to the expression of views that reflect the public mind on this issue. Some submissions, because of their very biased and partisan accent, we are forced to discount, but there have been several organizations that represent a fair cross-section of informed public thought on this question which should not be overlooked. I wish to quote from one or two of these submissions because I feel they come very close to expressing my own convictions in this respect.
I should like to quote from a resolution passed at a joint meeting of the council for social services and the executive council of general synod of the Anglican Church of Canada held in Toronto November 13, 1958. This represents one of the largest religious bodies in Canada. The resolution is as follows:
Whereas the Anglican Church of Canada has on several occasions expressed agreement with the Lambeth conference statement of 1948 to the effect that basic human rights should be "declared by the church, recognized by the state, and safeguarded by international law", and
Whereas the Canadian government has introduced a bill of rights in the House of Commons entitled, "An act for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms",
The council for social service in annual session reaffirms its approval in principle of a declaration of human rights for all Canadians.
I should now like to read from a submission made by one of the smallest religious bodies, the Seventh Day Adventist Church in Canada. This church took the time to study the matter very thoroughly and apparently spared no pains in an effort to express the collective thinking of its communicants on this subject for the benefit of the government and this house. This is a relatively small Christian church but it is the very inability of this church to speak as a majority group that lends a unique and significant import

to these observations. I now quote from their brief submitted to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) on January 9 of last year, copies of which brief were sent, I believe, to all hon. members:
The passage of a bill of rights reinforced and improved to the limit of present constitutional abilities will undoubtedly serve as one more powerful weapon in the arsenal of human liberty. We pray that it might be the best that human hands and hearts can devise. Human liberty requires constant vigilance and effort for its preservation and enlargement.
At page 5 of their submission they say:
We believe that the government is to be congratulated for its action in bringing down such a measure in parliament and for having taken time to ascertain the views of organizations and individuals with respect to this subject before submitting the bill to parliament for final legislative action. We applaud the genuine concern for human rights that this action and consequent procedures reveal.
And again at page 6:
We fully recognize that this measure is a first step along a long road, and we applaud the efforts of the government to take the initiative in leading Canada on this significant path to freedom. We ask that no effort be spared to see that other necessary steps are taken without undue delay.
Here we see the type of constructive, critical analysis that should characterize our deliberations at all times, but particularly when we are considering a measure that goes far beyond the bounds of our usual routine, partisan approach to the nation's business and welfare. I believe that these submissions from which I have just quoted outline a patriotic and rational attitude that commends itself to all hon. members.
This is not the occasion for the time-honoured pastime of shadow boxing in the ring of political aspirations. Let us be quite frank. This bill has its shortcomings, it is not perfect, it could contain other features that would reflect our deep longing for the firmest and most positive assurances that personal freedom shall for all time be secure. But we live in an imperfect world. We sojourn in an imperfect society. The important point which we must not overlook, though I fear that my hon. friends opposite with their tendency to see only the short term advantages are likely to neglect, is that Canada is moving forward along the long path toward the sunlit highlands of peace, justice, order and liberty in the widest measure for all Canadians.
Let us just note the gains that have been made. We have our solid foundation of Anglo-Saxon tradition and common law as a sound and true base for liberty's temple. The outstanding contribution over the years of our courts has given to this great edifice of freedom the sturdy yet beautiful walls it must have in a long and distinguished series of decisions that have served to reinforce the 79951-0-3741
Human Rights
shrine of liberty. Now we are called upon to take the first steps in providing the roof of the great shrine of Canadian liberty.
Are there any who feel that it is wise to try to erect the whole roof all at once? Is liberty deserving of only a prefabricated shelter? I should think not. It must have nothing but the best; and the best comes only after patient, thorough effort. It does seem strange that there are groups who, for reasons best known to themselves, fear to take a forward step because in one step they cannot encompass the whole journey. To these fearful hearts I would commend the words of some of our great national heroes. I am reminded of a statement that that great French Canadian patriot, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, once made when he was speaking in Montreal:
I have devoted my career to the realization of an idea. I have taken the work of confederation where I found it when I entered political life, and determined to give it my life, and nothing will deter me from continuing to the end in my task to preserve at all price our civil liberty.
I commend the words of this great Canadian mentor to his present-day political heirs. They would do well to imbibe some of the courage and vision of this man. Indeed, as one other great patriot, D'Arcy McGee, said:
We are in the rapids and must go on.
Canada finds itself in the rapids and if the precious cargo of freedom, yes life itself, is to be preserved from the swirling, treacherous currents of our times, we must go on in our search for the calm though strong and flourishing havens that liberty deserves.
It has been said, with a great deal to commend it, that we need, along with this bill, a bill of responsibilities. Ever since confederation we have been spelling out the responsibilities, the duties of Canadian citizens in every session of parliament and in the longer list of provincial legislatures. Now it is high time we gave to Canada, as a first step, a bill of rights that will clearly declare to all Canadians, present and future, the course of the road we have set our faces to travel toward.
I have not heard of hon. members complaining too effectively when some progressive piece of legislation is introduced in this house, by whatever government of Her Majesty, that unless we can have the whole scheme in its perfect ideal we shall have none of it. Yet this is the very type of questionable argument that some would have us believe should be accepted as the evidences of real statesmanship. Let us avoid that discreditable brand of doubtful statesmanship in this house.
So I say to you, sir, and through you to my compatriots, let us give Canada this bill

Human Rights
of rights now. Let us bring to this hour of Canada's history a largeness of heart and mind that can match the greatness of our land. Let us unite, despite the artificial bonds of race, tongue or creed, as Canadians, unhyphenated Canadians. Let us work together to make Canada one of the great fortresses of the free mind, of the liberated soul. In a world where the islands of true liberty are slowly but surely sinking into the oblivion of a dark and dismal sea of bigotry and hatred we should lay aside our party differences. This is a fine moment in Canada's history; it must see the finest in terms of our courage, our vision and our faith in the future. I am sure we shall all register that confidence by supporting this bill, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to be able to make some remarks on Bill C-79. I will not have to make a historical review of the rights and freedoms that are already guaranteed to us by the Canadian constitution, at least implicitly, or by the Magna Carta, or even by the British custom that we have inherited, since many of my learned colleagues have already done so. But all the same, I would like to put on record my personal views on this bill.
Mr. Speaker, by a happy coincidence-I would even say by a providential coincidence -we are discussing a most important bill which every right-thinking citizen must consider because we are, at this time, in this modern twentieth century that has already been called the atomic age. At this historical moment, no true Christian could question the usefulness nor the need for a collective manifestation of our faith in democracy and in the integral respect of human rights.
The world today is witnessing extraordinary and significant events that are setting all mankind a-tremble. The famous summit conference, in which we had too naively placed so much hope, has been sabotaged in a deliberate and even insidious manner by the spokesman of international communism.
At this summit meeting of the major heads of the states which hoped in the final triumph of the peaceful aspirations of the great majority of human beings, international communism was represented. It shed its mask, indicating once again the lack of sincerity on the part of the leaders of this materialistic world that we could call topsyturvydom.

The representative of the materialistic ideology, which our century has to face, did not show himself imbued by the wish to be a good spokesman for the people of his country, deserving as these people are, because of the numerous trials they have endured throughout their history. He was mainly the spokesman of a political party which, by its own definition, is dedicated to the suppression of religion, the promotion of war between the classes, the support of atheism, leading through a relentlessly logical process to the debasement of mankind by completely denying all human rights in the countries submitted to its totalitarian rule.
History irrefutably proves that whenever man has risen against God, or against divine or natural law, he has, inevitably in the end, betrayed the basic freedoms, individual and general.
The struggle between good and evil did not start yesterday; it began in Paradise after the first fall of man. And since then, one generation after another had to fight and exercise a restless vigilance to safeguard the respect of human rights. The lot of humanity has improved since the coming of the Saviour, the Lord's son who made himself man but, unfortunately, there are still various areas on earth where the basic freedoms and rights of many are in practice completely denied, even if sometimes, taking a hypocritical attitude, some countries pretend to set up a bill of rights, which, anyhow, is in no way observed.
The abridged title of the legislation before us aims at the recognition of rights and freedoms. Apart from those rights and freedoms, there are also duties and responsibilities. Abuses in various fields are often the result of a wrong interpretation of freedom. Abuses are the cause of many evils and certain people interpret in their own way the freedoms and the rights of man, when it is in their own interest.
It is hard to put on the right track a distorted mind interpreting in its own way, disregarding its duties and responsibilities, the various laws that must govern a country. And, as explained in the house, there has been unfortunate examples of such distorted minds that have ruled the world at certain times in history, particularly since the beginning of our century. Justice and charity towards our fellow citizens are not the least of those things to which we must pay attention.
For all those reasons, as a Canadian citizen proud of my country, of its democratic

regime and, at all times, free to express my opinion, I support this bill introduced by our Prime Minister, the champion of minorities and human rights, and also because I recognize that all individuals, regardless of race, origin, colour, religion or sex, have inalienable rights.
Thus it is in upholding the rights of every citizen across the country that we shall build a strong, great and more united Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I deem it a great honour and privilege to take part in the discussion of the bill of rights. It is my opinion that we shall never have peace in the world and unity in Canada unless we can educate and develop more men of good will. The nations of the world are at present spending a large proportion of the fruits of their labour and toil in preparation for possible aggression on account of the lack of men of good will in sufficient numbers to rule our human destinies with freedom and justice. Not only are the peoples of the world maintaining armies and developing war machines which can annihilate life itself on earth but life lived under such perpetual tension becomes to many almost unbearable. A bill of rights under the circumstances is really a beacon toward which not only Canadians but people of all nations can look and take courage and inspiration for freedom and peace.
To my mind this is the most important legislation that this parliament or any parliament can pass. The bill by implication proclaims that one cannot be a true citizen unless he is imbued with the principles embodied in this bill of rights. The true citizen must be desirous of freedom and justice not only for himself but for his neighbours and for all citizens of the world.
Canada was blessed at an important turning point in its history, namely the capitulation of Quebec in 1759, with a number of men of good will as governors from Great Britain. These men through their sterling qualities of heart and mind have made it possible for Canadians to preserve the integrity of the land that we are able to enjoy today. Some of these men deserve to have their names proclaimed as perhaps the real architects of a united Canada. I refer to the first two governors, Governor Murray and Governor Carleton.
The great governor James Murray was the author of the ordinance establishing a civil court in Quebec. This ordinance admitted and allowed the French law and custom in all causes in the courts between natives of Canada and provided also for Canadian advocates to practise in this court. His high
Human Rights
quality of heart and sense of justice are apparent in a letter written by him to the lords of trade dated October 29, 1764. I quote:
My lords:
Little, very little, will content the new subjects but nothing will satisfy the licentious fanaticks trading here but the expulsion of the Canadians who are perhaps the bravest and the best race upon the globe, a race, who could they be indulged with a few privileges which the laws of England deny to Homan Catholicks at home, would soon get the better of every national antipathy to their conquerors and become the most faithful and most useful set of men in this American empire.
I flatter myself there will be some remedy found out even in the laws for the relief of this people. If so, I am positive the popular clamours in England will not prevent the humane heart of the king from following its own dictates. I am confident too my royal master will not blame the unanimous opinion of his council here for the ordinance establishing the courts of justice, as nothing less could be done to prevent great numbers from emigrating directly, and certain I am, unless the Canadians are admitted on juries and are allowed judges and lawyers who understand their language, His Majesty will lose the greatest part of this valuable people.
I have the honour to be with the greatest truth and regard,
My lords, your lordships'
James Murray
I should also like to quote a letter written by Governor Carleton in reply to a complaint of five members of the council, which letter is dated October, 1766. I quote in part:
But that there may be no further doubt I hereby make known to you, and I tooth have and will, on all matters which do not require the consent of council, call together such counsellors as I shall think best qualified to give me information: and further, that I will ask the advice and opinion of such persons, though not of the council, as I shall find men of good sense, truth, candour and impartial justice; persons who prefer their duty to the king and the tranquility of his subjects to unjustifiable attachments, party zeal and to all selfish mercenary means.
Again, in a letter to Lord Shelburne dated December 4, 1767, Carleton writes in part complaining of the legal system:
How far this change of laws, which deprives such numbers of their honour, privileges, profits and property, is conformable to the capitulation of Montreal and treaty of Paris; how far this ordinance, which affects the life, limb, liberty and property of the subject, is within the limits of the power His Majesty has been pleased to grant to the governor in council; how far this ordinance, which in a summary way declares the supreme court of judicature shall judge all cases, civil and criminal, by laws unknown and unpublished to the people, is agreeable to the natural rights of mankind, I humbly submit this much is certain that it cannot long remain in force without a general confusion and discontent.
These two men have laid by their good will, love of justice and freedom a solid foundation upon which a great and united Canada can prosper. Most of the speeches

Mr. Speaker, there is not much in the way of originality that I can bring to this long debate but I do feel it is a rather sad occasion in so far as there seems to be so much difference of opinion of a minor kind on various points in the bill. I have tried to approach the matter from the point of view of a schoolteacher who has taught Canadian history to students between the ages of 14 and 17 perhaps lectured them, I do not

know. When you look at the Canadian history that you must put over to a 14 or 17 year old boy or girl you do so in the hope that you are achieving some kind of citizenship indoctrination, some belief in the nation, the spirit of it and where it is going. You have a number of dates and acts upon which you hinge your course.
There is always the Quebec act. There is always Durham's report and the act of union. There is always 1848 and responsible government with Lafontaine and Baldwin as the architects. There is always confederation and Sir John A. Macdonald, Cartier and the British North America Act. You move on from there to the emergence of Canada as a nation, not any longer a colony, and to such matters as the naval bill. You treat with the conscription crisis, and what it means, as well as with such incidents as the Chanok affair in 1922; the Statute of Westminster; the Rowell-Sirois report, and all these sign posts because you are attempting to give to the student an awareness of the Canadian traditions.
I am trying to look at this from the point of view of a schoolteacher. We are going to have in 1960 a bill of rights. In looking at the bill of rights I try to ascertain what message you could take from it to put in a textbook for the students. If anyone has tried to teach history he would discover that the hardest thing to put over is what responsible government is in essence. I have known teachers who have taught that lesson a dozen times a year and who have never been able to get a satisfactory response at the end of that time.
I wanted to turn to another type of history or another class of history that we teach that is much easier to put over and that is either United States or British history. United States history is taught in grades 9 and 10 in Ontario and is associated with Canadian history, as is British history. I think it has been regrettable that British history has not been separated. You get a mixing of the three. I find that the students apparently respond much more quickly and understandably to the signposts, the major points in United States and British history than they do to Canadian history. They can understand the declaration of independence or the Gettysburg address much more quickly than they do to the idea of responsible government or Durham's report. In so far as British history is concerned, you have the role of all the kings and of the great men of British history who tie things together. It is very difficult as a teacher of Canadian history to put forward Canadian heroes and make them stand in any kind of stature against the figures of United States history.
Human Rights
This is why it is always so disappointing to all of us after our students have passed out into the world that they are much more aware of Washington, Lincoln and Jefferson than they are of our own great figures. This is one of the reasons they can tell you about Nelson or even Napoleon; they have some idea even where a person like Gladstone fits, but they cannot give you a response to a Canadian figure. This question of the dullness of our history and of the inability of those of us who teach it to put it over, to make it live with vigour is something that bothers every one of us who has tried to do the job. We can think of all kinds of reasons to excuse ourselves and to excuse the nation itself.
It is with this sense of frustration and dissatisfaction that I have to look at this bill and to see how I, as a teacher, if I were preparing a textbook, could possibly fit this into our social studies or our history texts. I believe we have something that is going to be just as difficult to sell-I use the word "sell" not in the modern merchandising sense -as responsible government because there is no ringing preamble to this bill of rights. There is nothing of literary merit about it. It seems to be largely an exercise in legality and the sadness, as I pointed out at the start, is that we are continuing the typical Canadian difficulty.
Somehow, we seem to be the heirs of two traditions, the United States and Britain. We seem to be strangled by both. We get so much from both and yet when it comes to something like this we are back in the old position of compromise of our sovereignty and allegiances, a complete mix-up of jurisdictions in the country and a lack of unanimity. Despite all the nice things, the kind things that have been said in this house about human freedoms, it is a sad thing that we cannot have a short, pithy document, something that we could give to the young people of the nation.
Of course, you can look to other things that we have not obtained for our young people. We have not a national flag and some say we have not a national anthem. However, we are now going to be able to say that in 1960 we have a bill of rights which was introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), that it has been of great interest to him for a long time, that some amount of dissatisfaction was felt with regard to the bill but that the government felt that this was the best that could be done at the present time.
May I underline why this situation is so sad. The British tradition that we have, with the respect the British people have for the individual, is something that is different from

Human Rights
that of the Americans. Having lived in England for four years I always think of the British as being deferential people, as tending more along the line of deference, more along the line of great respect for the other person and having an attitude of fair play that is incomparable. It cannot be found elsewhere in the world, in my opinion. This spirit of fair play and of respect for others is one of the reasons why there is no need for them to have any formal statement. They can go back to the evolution of their parliamentary institutions. The institutions that Great Britain built around parliament have always tended to dominate the individual.
This is in contrast, it seems to me, with American history. The British in their sense of fair play and individual freedom have been historically oriented. They have always looked back to signposts. I have already expressed the difficulty that one has as a Canadian history teacher in looking back on Canadian history for our signposts. They just have not the colour or the force. The debt we owe to Britain is great. As the heirs of that tradition I hope we really do not need a bill of rights in that sense and that we can show fair play and respect for the other person, type of persons like the British, and that this bill to a degree is merely supernumerary.
Aside from the British tradition, we also get something from the North American environment by living close to what I think is a much more revolutionary country than soviet Russia ever has been or ever will be. I refer to the American nation with its emphasis upon equality and egalitarianism. One can be quite shocked with the contrast between British respect for form and dignity and American lack of it. The tendency of the American is that he wants to knock people down, and always to insist "I am as good as you are or any other man". But over the years it has become a very powerful force in our attitude toward human freedom. I would tend to suggest now that we share much more the American attitude toward human rights than we do the British one. In other words, I think we are now tending to be in the American revolution tradition rather than in the British evolutionary tradition in our attitude toward freedoms and rights.
The Americans have not been an historically minded people, although they have built up historical myths especially about their great men and hold in great respect people like Washington and Lincoln and the other great figures of their history. But all this emphasis in the United States has tended to be on a couple of exceptional personal

statements and upon great figures in their history. American history is always so exciting even today because most Canadians believe that Americans of this time are going to toss up another great figure who is going to crystallize the thinking of the nation and redirect the nation on a new path. It is a great cause of envy on my part that they should have this characteristic and that we should not have it.
Because of this problem of being confused by always being between these two traditions and never being sure where we are we are left with the sad kind of compromise that we have here at the present time, namely a bill that in my opinion, in a literal sense, is almost inarticulate. I am sure it is legally correct. It is certainly very cautious and it is rather incomplete in its statements of freedom.
I tried to search for reasons why we must be so cautious, why we cannot break into the American tradition that is based so much upon the declaration of independence and the self-evident truths or why we cannot be satisfied with the evolutionary idea that has come from our British stock. I think we must go back in our history to the failure of the French revolution to have had its impact upon our fellow Canadians of French stock. It was one of the great freedom breathing episodes of whole world history, and the fact that our French Canadian compatriots tended to deny the French revolution has left them and us with a minority position that does not look at freedom in either the American revolution way which is close to the French revolution way or is only partly in the British tradition. It seems to me that until we have reached the stage where they can share more in the revolutionary concept that I think other Canadians are tending to feel, we are going to be blessed or cursed, however you want to look at it-I cannot be that strong and say "cursed"-with the kind of bill of rights we have which is a compromise.
Recently I was in Saskatchewan after the election, not before it, and I had opportunity to talk for three days to and with a group of people who were from all political parties. They were generally discussing the question of Canadian democracy and whether it could survive. In respect of Saskatchewan I must say that I think I have never met anywhere else in Canada a body of people who seemed to be so knowledgeable, to have so much common sense and to be willing to accept their responsibilities as citizens; and this particular question of the need for a bill of rights was raised a number of times. I thought one

of the people in the discussion made a contribution that put the question for me.
He said he was not worried too much about impingement upon freedom but he wondered how we would react if his challenge really came. If we had some personality who was able so to dominate the national scene that he could begin to take over by regulation and, with the backing of the R.C.M.P. and the armed services, really begin to change us and direct us toward a kind of dictatorial government and situation that has not been part of our tradition, he wondered what we would do. He said: I wonder whether there are enough people in Canada who could go and get a gun and be prepared to fight.
This again is something that we have not had in our tradition, namely enough people or any people who were prepared to get a gun and go and fight. The Americans have their John Brown and "John Brown's Body". The British have their examples of the glorious revolution of 1688. We have had minor upsets like that of 1837 but it was a tragic and pitiful little affair. There was no great response. We showed very little fight in attaining whatever it is we have attained in the way of human freedom. I still feel that what the question will come down to in the future is whether we really have the freedoms that are set out in this bill, is whether we are prepared to respond immediately to the challenge and to fight for them.

The province ot Quebec has been, in the history of our country, a stronghold of individual and human freedoms.
For instance, I represent, for the most part, a population of new Canadians, all people that I meet very often, and they never miss an opportunity of reminding me that they would not want to live under other skies than those of Quebec. Because, they say, it is in that province that they have experienced their full personal development and in that same province that they have known the benefit of complete freedom.

Duties and rights are correlative. However, the obligation to respect the equal right of his fellows forbids man to make arbitrary use of his rights.
